utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good morning, everyone. Yes, Mr. Harvey.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President, Your Honours. May I introduce Julie Malingreau, who is -- has been with my team since September. She is from Belgium and holds a master's from the University of Amsterdam and also a master's from the University of Louvain-la-Neuve.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Ms. Edgerton, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Matovic. Can you understand me?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR MATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning. Yes, I do understand.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I'm not going to keep you too long today, but I'd like to ask you a couple of questions based on some of the things you said yesterday and the statement you signed for Dr. Karadzic's team.

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR MATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: All right. Now, yesterday you were explaining Mr. Cosic's position on the arrest of Mr. Izetbegovic, following the publication of the Islamic Declaration. And you had got, if you remember that, to the point where you were explaining how Izetbegovic's wife came with the families of those who had been arrested and brought some money, and then you were interrupted. So, Mr. Matovic, without getting into more detail about -- are you all right, sir?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR MATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Without getting into more detail about what you were saying yesterday, I just want to ask you, it's actually correct, isn't it, that in the context of the forum established in Belgrade to protect freedom of speech, Mr. Cosic spoke out in support of non-Serbs under arrest. That's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR MATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would kindly ask that I tell you once again in my own words what my recollection is and what I actually said. Maybe it was a slip of the tongue on my part. May I repeat what I said yesterday. No money, for heaven's sake, no. Mr. Cosic to receive it or in any way -- I mean, really. I hope that in most of the world that would be the greatest possible offence, if somebody would offer you that kind of thing. Right now a campaign against corruption is under way in the country, but really, for a man to hold such high office -- well, he wasn't president yet at that time. But still, for him to do that kind of thing, no. At sessions of his own committee, he lodged a protest with the authorities. This was in Belgrade, but it was actually in Sarajevo that the arrest took place, and even I as a journalist was involved in order to write about that, and I said to my own paper -- actually, it was my newspaper and the Sarajevo official newspaper "Oslobodjenje" that was supposed to write about this together. I talked to Izetbegovic and I understood, according to my journalistic knowledge in terms of responsibility and guilt and freedom of expression, my understanding was that there was nothing criminal about what he did, simply that it was his right, because he just claimed that this Islamic Declaration was his religious belief, not anything that had to do so with statehood. That's what Cosic said at the committee's session. He lodged a protest. I mean, I cannot even remember anymore. I mean, he lodged so many protests in Belgrade. He didn't want to go to Sarajevo, he didn't want to interfere in their affairs, but this was a protest. How can someone be prosecuted for expressing his religious beliefs? And then part of the press that was more liberal, sort of, at the time and the families heard about this and the wives, that is to say, the wife of Alija Izetbegovic and -- but look, look. They came home and they brought these gifts that were very sweet, you know oriental sweets, small gifts. Now, the Cosics -- well, he organised a luncheon close to his house. I can't remember now -- I mean, if it really matters to you, I can even try to remember the restaurant where the luncheon was held, and I know that during that conversation Professor Ljubomir Tadic was present, too, because he came from Sarajevo. He was more familiar with the situation there and -- so there was this conversation and Cosic said what he had to say because we Serbs, after all -- well, at the time they claimed amongst the Sarajevo public that all of this came from Belgrade through -- well, and so on and so forth. But he energetically denied that and now I, to the best of my knowledge, think that this is something that really cannot be linked to him as a person and to all the work that he authored. I don't know if you're understanding what I'm saying.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Matovic. I'm understanding perfectly and you've answered my question and clarified what you said yesterday. Now, I just want to turn to specifically some things you said in your statement. Now, if I understand your written statement correctly, your evidence as regards Srebrenica, your evidence is that the mass execution in July 1995 of over 7.000 Bosnian men and boys by the armed forces of Republika Srpska was preplanned, preplanned - because that's what we take from your statement - preplanned in an international conspiracy involving German officers -- pardon me, American and German officers and politicians with whom the VRS were in contact. That's what you said in your statement. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR MATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, I was either under the influence of some kind of drugs or drink. I don't drink as a rule, but something like that. Really, I kindly ask you to read that out to me. I did not read my statement after I gave it and I cannot believe that. I mean, really. I crossed the Drina and I'm rushing from Zvornik to find out and to inform my bosses, my employers, about what was going on there. The only thing I was told was that in Srebrenica, it seems that some old woman, somebody unofficially said that to me, I mean the people who were far away from Srebrenica, even Han Pijesak and so on and so forth -- well, yes. Will that do? Would that be enough for you?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Well, what I'll do is I'll -- I'll do what you asked and I'll read you what your statement says. All right. And --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Let's upload the statement.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I don't have the exhibit number. It was 1D09095.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Exhibit D4184.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Could the witness have hard copy, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll see. It's very short.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Registry can print out the B/C/S version.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Yes. And for the B/C/S version we should go over to page 2.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Sir, we'll print out your statement in hard copy. Bear with us a minute.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Mr. Matovic, I think to see what I put to you, I think you need to look at the bottom of the first paragraph on page 2. And I'll read it out so that perhaps you can find it a bit more easily, and this is about your meeting with Nadja. Nadja, you said, told you about the danger posed by -- Nadja --

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR MATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: She told you about "the danger posed by NATO 'hawks' grouped around some American and German officers and individual politicians" --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could we please have the exact place in B/C/S. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will try to answer if I understood you correctly now. Nada was not --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Could I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Wait for the question. It's page 2 in English.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I beg your pardon. I do apologise.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And, I'm sorry, I'm just trying to find the exact page in Srpski -- or the exact line reference in Srpski for the interpreters. If you could just give me a moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, it's the bottom part of the first paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Yes, I think it's the -- perhaps the fifth or sixth line up from the bottom of the first paragraph.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, I see it. Fifth line from the -- yes, there, in inverted commas. Why don't you read out from an earlier part so that the witness can understand. But I leave it to you. Mr. Matovic, did you find the passage?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I found it. "From Han Pijesak he went to Pale," is that the beginning of the paragraph?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I don't think he's found it --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I be of assistance. The previous paragraph, Nadja said to him further on --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This other paragraph, Nadja -- oh, yes, yes, sorry. "Nadja also said to him -- told him of the danger posed by the NATO 'hawks' grouped around some American and German officers and individual politicians who were regularly in touch through several intelligence agencies with a number of VRS officers. She also warned him that preparations were being made for mass killings of Muslims, especially civilians, to serve" -- now this is what I point out -- so this is a sentence depending on its second clause, so to speak, "to serve as a justification for the already planned NATO operation to attack Republika Srpska." So the first part of the sentence, its beginning -- well, I mean unless you read the entire sentence. Nadja's brief information was that. It was a warning, it was an appeal, not to go into -- well, during the conflict things did happen, I can tell you specifically what and where, so that -- not to do anything that the "hawks" and NATO would use in order to bomb Republika Srpska. I don't know if I was clear and I don't know if this would suffice for your purposes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Well, it doesn't seem like when you gave your statement you were clear because this statement alleges that the mass executions at Srebrenica by the Bosnian Serb military were preplanned, preplanned, in a conspiracy involving the Americans and the Germans. And that the VRS seems to have been aware of it?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR MATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: May I answer by reminding you of what I said yesterday. The warning that she brought was that now the greatest danger for the Serbs is the revanchism of our traditional enemy, Germany; namely, after the Muslim offensive failed, it was abating by then and it did not yield the results that they had promised their financiers and weapons donors, there was a danger of new provocations from the Muslim side. If they manage to stage some kind of revenge or anything that the Serbs would carry out, then, then, that would serve their purposes even more because this would be a justification for NATO to carry out bombing if the Serb forces bomb or in any other way imperil -- I don't know if the interpreters are going to understand this word of ours, that is frail people, frail people, that is to say, women, children, old men. And later on, that is what was being done on the Serb side by way of a reaction. Could you please explain these details to me. I mean, I'm looking at this and -- yes --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Matovic -- Mr. Matovic, it's me.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I'm asking you, Mr. Matovic, take a look at the last sentence in the first paragraph. I will read it out to you again: "She also warned him," "him" being you, "that preparations were being made for mass killings of Muslims ..." You said here that prepare -- she said to you "that preparations were being made for mass killings ..." so this is a wrong formulation according to your words right now, according to your explanation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I do apologise. I didn't want to interrupt you. In the version that I've been given, I don't seem to be able to find this --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Excellencies, problem is with the translation. Probably for the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. I would ask the interpreters to interpret as they are hearing, not according to this English version. Could you read out the last sentence in the above -- in the first paragraph, after the "NATO 'hawks' ..."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Hawks? Oh, yes, the next sentence, right? "He was with Nadja very briefly" --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Oh, so I repeat this. Right? "She also said to him that Alija Izetbegovic also gave approval to take -- to have Srebrenica taken by the VRS and that to that end Naser Oric received orders that" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Could you take a look at the monitor. Our usher will indicate with a cursor. Do you see the sentence here on the monitor, "Nadja"?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Excellency, he just started to read this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, could you read out from there.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes, I see it now. "Nadja further on said to him that there is a danger of, as she said, certain politicians -- politicians" --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You skipped a line, you skipped a line, I beg your pardon. A line was skipped.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] "Nadja further on said to him that there was a danger of, as she said, hawks in NATO gathered around part of American and German officers and certain politicians and who are in constant contact through a few intelligence services with a certain number of VRS officers, and that what is being prepared is a more massive suffering of the Muslim population, especially civilians, so that that would be a justification for the already-planned operation of NATO to attack Republika Srpska." Now, do you want me to explain this yet again, this sentence? Would you want me to analyse the essence of this sentence in my view --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a minute, Mr. Matovic. Wait for the question. Thank you for your reading.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Maybe we could collapse the English version so that if Mr. Matovic has to look back to his statement it will be clearer to him.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So, Mr. Matovic --

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR MATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: -- there was no conspiracy - that's what you're telling us?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR MATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Did he say ever there was a conspiracy?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: No, that was my question to him, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Mr. Matovic, do you accept, then, that in July 1995, members of the Bosnian Serb Army and the Bosnian Serb police executed more than 7.000 Bosnian men and boys? Do you accept that? That's true, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR MATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I never came across such suggestive, leading questions. If the point of Nadja's arrival and my conversation with her and -- I mean, I have this experience as a journalist when I receive information, the most important thing for me is whether the person involved is well-intentioned, competent. I would have had further questions, but I didn't put any questions to her. She saw the expression on my face when she started talking about what was going on in NATO, new attacks, et cetera. She probably saw the look on my face and then expanded this sentence. She did not ask me about the number of casualties --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: No -- no --

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR MATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- and whether there were any conflicts and I did not know. I came from the other side of the Drina River --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Mr. Matovic, now, now, almost 20 years after the fact, do you accept that Bosnian Serb military and police perpetrated the mass executions of over 7.000 Bosnian men and boys in Srebrenica in July 1995? Do you accept that now as true?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR MATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I accept, but not with a yes or no. I accept it with a short explanation, if you would allow me just two sentences in reply.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Please carry on, Mr. Matovic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] To this day, many things remain unclear to me, although I have spent perhaps more time there than most Yugoslav journalists and politicians and have spent a lot of my time trying to explain to others the gist of this conflict. And still today my colleagues, journalists, reporters, approach me asking for a briefing, for an explanation, but still some essential things remain unclear to me. One of the most unclear things to me is how a small town such as Srebrenica which, statistically, according to censuses had 8- to 10.000 population and 300 houses. Who are the 7.000 men, fighting men, who came there and who was executed? I know the birth-rate used as a policy that they had taken over from the Albanians --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Mr. Matovic --

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR MATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- the elevated birth-rates that are the strongest weapon against Europeans --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just let him continue --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Apologies, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: -- and see how far he goes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Please continue, Mr. Matovic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So for me to answer such questions from someone who's coming from Belgrade to receive a message and for that person to communicate to Nadja because even with my close friends who share my views and opinions about the situation in the world and especially on the borders of our country -- I mean, what kind of fighting -- I was even told that there was not much fighting in Potocari, that the battalion had pulled out and the civilians followed the battalion because they had been promised asylum and employment in the United States, in Europe, et cetera; whereas the army was there at first, and the first one to leave was Naser Oric - I don't know if that's in my statement - and he was followed by other military able-bodied men who headed for Zepa and other enclaves under their control, their bases.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Do you remember the question, Mr. Matovic? So your answer is: Yes?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Did I convey to Nadja or anyone else that the Serbs had killed there 7.000 Muslims? I hear such a round figure for the first time. Later on, there were claims from the Muslim side to that effect, but I learned about it gradually more from the media than directly, although I continued visiting Republika Srpska --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The question was: As you sit here now today, do you accept that about 7.000 Muslims were killed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I cannot accept something, especially not in the form of my statement, something that I don't know about. The only thing I do know is that from all theatres of war in Yugoslavia at that time, in Croatia, in Bosnia-Herzegovina, in Kosovo and Metohija later, every party to that war tended to maximise its losses, the civilians who were killed, unlike some previous wars where commands used to minimise their losses. In this war, every side --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Matovic --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- exaggerated the numbers of casualties and dead.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I think you answered the question, but before Ms. Edgerton continues. Mr. Robinson, having seen such a discrepancy between the original and English translation, I can't see how Ms. Edgerton can continue her cross-examination. I'm not sure whether the other part -- the translations of other parts are correct. So I would like to first ask who prepared this, who translated?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: The Registry's language section.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Probably I would ask the witness to tell us live, from the beginning till the end, about his contact with Nadja. How you came to meet her and what you talked -- the conversation with her and what you did in Han Pijesak. Could you tell us, as far as you remember. Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In Han Pijesak with Nadja -- no. I met with her in Zvornik --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Let me ask you then. So could you explain to us how you came to meet Nadja first?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I noticed her because, you must understand, I was much younger then. I noticed her in the entourage of General Gallois, who travelled to Romania rather often in that period, and for various reasons and various errands he often stopped by in Belgrade. He would call us in advance from Bucharest or Timisoara. But you understand I'm not an investigator or a prosecutor, and I didn't know that I would have to testify about this later. But he asked mostly for books, materials, our information that we had about the developments in our state, in our country as it was then, and our current Western neighbours, former Yugoslav republics --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Let me help you. Did Mr. Bulatovic ask you to meet Nadja?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, he didn't ask for that. Officially I think he was even on vacation, and when that meeting was held, he said I should go because I know the situation very well, whereas he was a Montenegrin who was not really involved in that, not well informed. He learned more later but not at that time. I don't even know what the phrasing was. He was simply looking for a person who was not too busy and he said it would be good if I could go. You know, July is a time when people go on holiday, and at that time I was still able to go on holiday with my family. I think you understand what I'm talking about. So I didn't really feel like going to Srebrenica; I wasn't keen on it. I had things to do with my family, but out of the three of them I was the least busy and that's why I accepted. There were no orders involved or it was not interference, and as far as I remember, he told me: It would be good if you, Vlada, could go because you know the people, you know the situation --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Excellency, if I may --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No, just a second. We'll see how this witness can answer this question and see -- we'll consider whether this witness should be led live from the outset. Mr. Matovic, did you meet Nadja at the Vidikovac restaurant? Do you remember the meeting?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Of course, on the terrace of that motel called Vidikovac, overlooking the lake.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So could you begin your story from there. What did you talk about with Nadja?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There's no story. I was not in any kind of position to consider with her --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: My apologies -- no --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- and deliberate --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No, it's my mistake. Could you tell us what you heard from Nadja at that restaurant?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that in this statement, although I can't read it all now, it is described clearly --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No, just a second --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- she started saying things that were --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Without relying on your statement, could you tell us as far as you remember what you heard from Nadja at that restaurant?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Encounters with persons of that kind - because she was not a politician or a military strategist, just as I was not - from my personal experience, both as a journalist and later from working in the office of the president, was as follows. Ultimately an impression is created, although things got very confused, that there is something that I should convey. She told me exactly what is said in this statement --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- I don't know if there is a translation issue --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- but I can tell you, I can repeat what she said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Ms. Edgerton, did you want to say something?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: That he was reading his statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: But, Excellencies, I would like you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Given that his statement is very short, I think he should be led live.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Excellencies, I would like you to see the last sentence that you didn't get translation, since you have been conferring. He can repeat what she said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: He's reading his statement. Unfortunately, the Chamber is not satisfied that this statement should be admitted into evidence pursuant to Rule 92 ter. I will consult my colleagues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, could the witness be excused for a moment. Mr. Matovic, if you could excuse yourself for a moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: In light of the discrepancy, first, between the original and the English translation and, secondly, his statement and his oral testimony, the Chamber is of the view it is fair enough to -- for the witness to be led live, if Mr. Karadzic is to call him as his witness. But if he wishes, in light of these circumstances, he may reschedule his evidence later on if he so wishes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, Mr. President, I think that -- because this witness is old and it's very difficult for him to make this trip, we'll just go ahead and lead his evidence live and we'll just try to settle the bill with you later as to how the hours would be allocated for that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: But, Mr. Robinson, isn't the real difficulty going to be if this witness is -- he's an elderly gentleman, he's trying to recall things that happened 20 years ago, he seems to be having difficulty remembering independent of the statement. If he's not going to be using the statement as it is, and it seems he can't because of the translation issues, in reality is this something you want to advise Dr. Karadzic -- have five minutes to advise Dr. Karadzic on as to whether or not there is any realistic benefit to the Defence in continuing with this witness as matters stand?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, it's always good to consider things, but frankly, this witness is here because he met Dr. Karadzic in July 1995 and says Dr. Karadzic didn't have very good information about Srebrenica. So I think we could lead that part of the evidence live and Ms. Edgerton can deal with the rest of it as far as I'm concerned. But we can discuss that and see if that's what Dr. Karadzic wants to do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Do you have any observation, Ms. Edgerton?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: If I can -- if I may just note, Mr. President, I think Mr. Robinson attempted to put a kind of marker down which I can't imagine the Court shares, and that is "we'll settle the bill later," as if this is somehow the Chamber's responsibility. So I don't think that should be entered into the record as if some kind of concord was struck between Mr. Robinson and the Chamber and it will be thrashed out later. I don't think that's the Court's intention at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Could I ask --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Would you like to --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Could I ask about -- could the general questions about first and second paragraph be admitted, not to be repeated?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: No, the witness said: I didn't read my statement after my gave it. So no, under no circumstances, I would think.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Would you like us to rise for some time to discuss it with Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, that would be good. If we could take a five-minute recess.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we'll resume at 10.00. --- Break taken at 9.53 a.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karadzic or Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, we will make our best effort to lead the witness live at this time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. So what we are going to do is to vacate the admission of his statement pursuant to 92 ter. So we'll vacate the number as well, but what remains will remain on the transcript and we'll hear the witness live. Very well. Shall we bring in the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good morning again, Mr. Matovic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: There is an issue with translation and something else, so we -- the Chamber has decided to hear your evidence orally instead of through your written statement. So Mr. Karadzic will ask you questions. Do you follow? Do you understand that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Please bear in mind just one thing. Because Mr. Karadzic and you are speaking the same language, you need to put a pause between the question and answer. Therefore, please wait for some time after he posed his question before you start your answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Excellencies. Good morning to everybody.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Matovic.

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR MATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This was too fast. Please make a longer pause. Mr. Matovic, let's forget about any statements. Could you please tell us whether you met me in July 1995?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR MATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In July 1995, whether I met you at all?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Were you in my office in July 1995?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR MATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you remember what we discussed at that time?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR MATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me just say one thing, I met you when I was pressed for time, and it was on two occasions. The first time was around Srebrenica, around that operation, and later it was around the events in the Republic of Croatia and Republika Srpska. We met twice briefly. The first time with regard to Srebrenica and I told you that -- or rather, I don't remember whether I told you about a link that existed between the two of us. I don't know whether I explained to you who that was. I told you that I had information. I'm confused that -- with certain things. I don't know whether some of the text for my future books have been preserved -- hold on, hold on, let me just tell you this. I have never told anybody about that meeting with Nadja. I never said to anybody whether she asked me about war operations. I don't know where she had come from. I never asked her in our relations. It is not polite. Any subsequent question questions the credibility of that person if you speak about their intentions.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Matovic, let's ignore that. The statement is off the table. Can you remember what the two of us discussed and did you establish what I knew? Did I establish what you knew about Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR MATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not the one who could inform you because I did not have any information about these events. I only told you that we had a benevolent source and that we received information from that source that there had been a breakup in NATO, that there had been a rift in NATO, and that after a lull and after the end of the Muslim offensive, some of the representatives said that the war was futile and that the Serbs were already holding over 70 per cent of the territory. But it was not what I heard from Nadja. Nadja told me what I said in my written statement. There was rift in the top echelons of NATO, there were divisions into hawks and pigeons, i.e., those who were in favour for those -- for the continuation of the war and -- on the one hand and the others who didn't want a war, who did not want to go on paying for those senseless wars.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. When it comes to the events in Srebrenica, did you ask me anything and how much I knew about all that?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR MATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I expected from you to tell me because I was a journalist, I had not returned to you with her message because as a journalist that would have seemed that I had been there, and at the same time I did not document any of that because my conversation with her, all of the information that I received from her, I knew that she had brought that information from either The Hague or Brussels. I don't know where from. And the message was just a warning and an appeal --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR MATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: She wanted to prevent us from falling into a trap.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you. Let's ignore Nadja.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. We can continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Matovic, let's not mention Nadja at all. What did the two of us discuss? Did you ask me anything? Did you inform me about anything? What did I ask you?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR MATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I remember --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- from that conversation --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: With respect, Your Honour, Dr. Karadzic should be particularly careful in formulating his questions for this question, given what's gone on previously, and he should refrain from piling it on, as he's been doing, in a leading manner.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Let me help you. Mr. Matovic, do you remember meeting Mr. Karadzic in July 1995?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I remember -- may I continue?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: My question was whether you remembered having met Mr. Karadzic in July 1995. The answer could be either yes or no.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Do you remember how many times you met Mr. Karadzic in July 1995.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I remember that meeting and an attempt to meet him. I had some letters to give him but I didn't meet with him, but with his clerk in the offices of the Presidency of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. He was not there, nobody knew when he was coming back. I had some letters which I left with his secretary, like many times before.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So you met once in July 1995 Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One correction, please. I no longer know what is a statement, what is a translated statement. I only know that we met twice, but I don't know whether that meeting was in July. I arrived with similar information, and the second time I met with Nadja who gave me information -- but I don't know whether that was in July or August. I really can't remember as I sit here today. I don't know whether it was towards the end of July. I can't remember when I shared with him the information about the Republic of Serbian Krajina and the preparations for that situation over there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So when you met Mr. Karadzic in July 1995, what did you discuss with Mr. Karadzic at the time? Could you tell us as far as you remember?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Most of which I remember was him talking about reliability. His main source of information was CNN. He asked me whether I knew anything about comments in the printed press because I was a journalist for "Politika" for a while and I followed wars and similar things. We exchanged opinions about that; however, I had arrived in his office to ask him what he knew about all that and whether he could inform those people and ask them what was correct, whether a war had indeed started, what its intensity was and so on and so forth. As far as I can remember, he told me that he was also told just like I was. The feedback that I received - and let me tell you, this is a bit morbid, a bit banal - that they were aware of an old woman who was a victim, but nobody spoke about 7.000 soldiers who were killed. That was unheard of, and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Back to you, Mr. Karadzic. You'll be better off if you ask one question at one time. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did we discuss some prisoners at the time during that meeting?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR MATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, much, much later there were talks about prisoners, and especially about those prisoners when President Cosic invited the Nobel Prize winner Elie Wiesel came to visit Belgrade, it was a humanitarian visit, and he wanted to receive information about camps where Muslims were detained in Bosnia and Herzegovina. Then I visited you again. You told me what you did and I conveyed that message to Mr. Wiesel. I said: Sir, where you think those camps are and if you have that information from Belgrade, you will not have any obstacles from Belgrade. I believe that his escorts can confirm that. Just a moment, please. There were helicopters, there were APCs where he went, and the rule was never to agree things well in advance, but on that morning when I arrived, then he would tell me where we were going and then I would take him there. There was fighting around most of the camps, but I'm telling you -- did you understand me? Are you happy with my answer?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR MATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Then we talked and you said that everything would be open to him. Of course, one had to look at the situation, Manjaca, around Gorazde, Foca, and Banja Luka, to see whether it was safe to go to those places.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you please tell us whether it transpired that I was well informed about the events that took place in Srebrenica in July 1995? When we met, did you gain the impression --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Before you answer the question, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: This is completely leading and inappropriate, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Can you reformulate your question.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Matovic, how well informed was I about the events in Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR MATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I repeat, when somebody says that they are informed mostly through CNN -- and as a professional I don't have anything against them, I follow CNN as well. However, if one has only one source of information and if you told me one sentence which I can only paraphrase and you said that you knew that there was an operation going on and that I could not take more information to Belgrade about the essence of those things and so on and so forth. And that's why at the end of that journey I myself tried to go there to get to Bratunac, to General Mladic, who was going to tell me perhaps -- and the others generals that I found in Han Pijesak, they were the logistics command and they claimed that they didn't know anything. And when I told them what was being written and what we saw on television, for example, they said that they didn't know anything about that, that they couldn't believe that. By way of illustration, I'm telling you this to illustrate the tone of that conversation. So when I brought those letters, I suppose that I brought some fresher information that we had received from other sides. I can't remember that for a fact. In this court, there were trials against the French, the Gaullis [phoen], who communicated with our military representatives and who provided them with information that you're asking me to give you today. I was not a military --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you please explain, you said that: "... I could not take to Belgrade information." Why you couldn't take any information from me to Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR MATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because, and this is exactly what I told them, that you were not well-informed or that you don't have enough information, and as far as I can remember, there is quite a distance between Srebrenica and Pale, and those formations passed through that then and before that, and it was not safe to go from Srebrenica to Pale. So I don't know when was it that your security would have allowed you to go there because I myself was warned, and it did happen to me, albeit later, when I was in the car with your director of the state bank, we passed by a Muslim column which was resting there. So I'm sure that they would not have allowed you to put yourself in such situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have no further questions for Mr. Matovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Mr. Matovic, when you met Dr. Karadzic and had a discussion with him, he didn't tell you anything about the information he was receiving about what was going on in Srebrenica from his soldiers, their commanders, his police, their commanders, members of the diaspora, the Serbian diaspora, and his local political officials. He didn't tell you anything about all the information he was receiving from them, did he?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR MATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Would you accept my attempt? I don't know how much you know about this. May I respond in a journalistic way, which is closer to me? Would that suit you?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Mr. Matovic --

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR MATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: -- I specifically formulated the question so you could answer it actually quite easily rather than in a journalistic way. My question was: He didn't tell you anything about all the other information he was receiving, did he? You could answer yes or no.

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR MATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I cannot. Quite simply, I didn't put questions like that to him. That's what I'm trying to tell you. If you have the patience -- as a reader of newspapers, you will understand. Am I allowed to answer in a specific, telling way?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could you be brief? Let's hear him, yes. Be brief, Mr. Matovic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll try to be as succinct as possible. I was a journalist for 40 years and then I lectured at the institute of journalism. I gave lectures to foreign students about the selection of information. I had surprising news from Nadja, front-page news. But when news is front-page news, then it has to be -- well, this time I was not a journalist. I was there as a rapporteur for the people who sent me there, to bring some news. And if I have an explanation -- now, whether I'm going to manage for this knowledge to be front-page news, all of it, or will something have to go to the other pages. But how could I when Mr. Karadzic said to me that he also, concerning the proportions of the conflict and this operation, whether it was a war operation or not, he said that at that point in time he did not know that, that he was not informed. I mean this is a set of circumstances and a person has to respond quickly, and one does not have the time -- well, the president of the republic -- after all, I was supposed to understand whether this information that I received -- whether I could have more details. I could -- I did not have the time to go to the front line, but also I was advised by the logistics command in Han Pijesak not to go. But not because of the operations but because the commander of the army, General Mladic, was constantly from Bijeljina, Zepa, this was war time, inaccessible. Now, whether they said this to me or not -- I mean, he had a helicopter. He had everything that was necessary. It was hard -- Well, that is what he advised me and --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Mr. Matovic?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR MATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So I take it from what you're saying that the answer to my question is: No, Dr. Karadzic didn't tell you anything about the information he was getting from other sources; right?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR MATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I cannot. Because I did not have the time to comment upon the situation at the front line. I asked him whether he knew what the intensity was. As for what Nadja said to me, could -- could I enrich that with some new knowledge? And he said no because he himself was insufficiently informed and did not know when he would receive relevant information.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: All right --

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR MATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And I was in a hurry and -- yes? Yes, please go ahead and sorry.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Your Honours, I note the time. If you'd like to take a break now, it would probably take me about seven minutes after we resume again. I could probably make things even shorter after a half an hour's reflection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we'll take a break for half an hour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. On reflection, I have no further questions of Mr. Matovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Edgerton. Do you have any re-examination?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Excellency. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Matovic, before we broke you said when you met Mr. Karadzic you said, I quote: "This time I was not a journalist. I was there as a rapporteur for the people who sent me there to bring some news." Could you clarify what you meant by this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I come from a profession that has its rules where I worked for 40 years, and then after a few months I found myself in the complete opposite in terms of the freedom of behaviour, activity, et cetera, that kind of profession, where other rules were in force. When I said that, that's what I meant. Also, there are some books, some people from Belgrade held it against me, colleagues, friends, said that while I was an official I was not open at all. And then we clarified the matter and they publicly apologised. From one profession I found myself in a completely different one that has its own rules. What is communicated to me -- I mean, it's not for me if an interlocutor communicates some information to me, and especially if they do not communicate some information to me, it's not for me to comment upon anything with the bearer of such information. So that's the only thing I meant. Her job was to bring information; my job was to convey information. And at that moment when I went to Mr. Karadzic and all that, for me -- after all, it was the journalist in me that surfaced. It was a sensational information, the content of that information, and so I tried with the two most competent persons to -- well, just as I did, contrary to the interests of the authorities, I was supposed to talk to Alija Izetbegovic as well, but I refused that because of certain convictions of my own, journalistic convictions. And now, when I was a civil servant working for the state, I got this sensational news, and for them it would be a sensation, too, but without anything to corroborate it. But I didn't have time then to go to Srebrenica or anywhere else. I just went to the top place to confirm or deny that. Quite simply, I was told what I was told, and as for the prosecutor's office and everyone else, I do apologise to all of you. It's not only against the moral, professional, and other rules in terms of what I did beforehand. But I think that anywhere, in any profession, even the most special police -- after all, people have to have certain boundaries and see how they're going to behave to who. I mean, you can treat a certain person as the president of the republic or not, but I have to because at that moment he is officially president of the republic. And I cannot ask the president of the republic: Tell me, how many dead are there down there, and so on? That's not my role, that's not my function, and professionally that was not allowed. At that place -- I mean there -- it's not that I'm trying to glorify the journalist professional in ethical terms or whatever, but there are some rules of conduct or rules of the game, if you will. So I cannot answer that, what it was that we talked about. We talked about -- I mean, I asked him whether he knew what the message was that was conveyed to me, whether approximately you see some looming danger, threat, not to play into the hands of the other side and so on and so forth. And his answer was that, unfortunately, he does not have enough, especially from all sides, and even there during the operations that he would follow, and that's how it all ended.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: When you met Mr. Karadzic, were you still working at the Presidency of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Oh, of course. Actually, in a way I was working, but I did not have a specific post. I was an official at large, if you will. It was, say, adviser for extraordinary situations. I did not have the post and office that I had when I was adviser to the president of the republic, but the Ministry of Defence then and later on during the war operations, NATO, that was called responding to foreign hostile propaganda.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. This is a question for the parties: Is the meeting of this witness with Mr. Karadzic reflected in his agenda? What -- if the parties could remind me of the date.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. President, the meeting is not reflected in the agenda.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: That's correct, it is not. And we don't have a date --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: -- of this meeting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Matovic, that concludes your evidence. On behalf of this Chamber, I would like to thank you for your coming to The Hague to give it. Please have a safe journey back home.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much indeed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Is there any further change to the witness schedule?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: No, Mr. President. The next witness is Mr. Milincic and he should be here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And then after him?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Kovacevic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And then?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: I don't believe we will reach Mr. Radinkovic, so then tomorrow we will start with Colonel Blagojevic and General Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Would the witness make the solemn declaration, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth. I would like to add something. May God help me as I speak.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Milincic. Please be seated and make yourself comfortable.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. Before you commence your evidence, Mr. Milincic, I must draw your attention to a certain rule of evidence that we have here at the Tribunal, that is, Rule 90(E). Under this rule, you may object to answering any question from Mr. Karadzic, the Prosecutor, or even from the Judges if you believe that your answer might incriminate you in a criminal offence. In this context, "incriminate" means saying something that might amount to an admission of guilt for a criminal offence or saying something that might provide evidence that you might have committed a criminal offence. However, should you think that an answer might incriminate you and, as a consequence, you refuse to answer the question, I must let you know that the Tribunal has the power to compel you to answer the question. But in that situation, the Tribunal would ensure that your testimony compelled under such circumstances would not be used in any case that might be laid against you for any offence, save and except the offence of giving false testimony. Do you understand that, Mr. Milincic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I understand perfectly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Mr. Karadzic, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good day, Professor Milincic.

utterances.speaker: MILOS MILINCIC
utterances.text: Good day. Good luck to you and God bless you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. It's going to be very hard for them to interpret that. It's a very old adage of ours, or rather, it's a verse from Njegos. I have to ask you something, let us pause between question and answer, and as we utter our sentences, we should try to be as slow as possible so that they would be recorded in the transcript. Could I kindly ask you to give us your name and surname, your father's name, your date and place of birth.

utterances.speaker: MILOS MILINCIC
utterances.text: Of course. Milos Milincic, professor of literature, retired. I live in Bajinci, in Banja Luka, right now. The 15th of December, 1942. I have a family, two children.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Milincic -- Milincic is the right spelling. Thank you. Tell us about your political and professional career. What were all the things you did?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MILINCIC
utterances.text: I worked as a professor in school. I taught the Serbian language and literature. I was the principal of an elementary school and then a high school. And in the elections in 1990, I was elected speaker of the Srbac Assembly according to the will of the citizens and political party. And then I was director of the educational institute in Banja Luka and I retired from there. As for party and ideological affiliation, I was a member of the League of Communists until 1990, from the time when I did my military service. And then in 1990 I became a member of the Serb Democratic Party.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. During your career, professional and political, were you commended, awarded? Did you receive any decorations?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MILINCIC
utterances.text: Yes, as a professor in school I won top prizes in the subject of language because pupils were tested every year in the region of the Krajina, Banja Luka, at the time. And I also have two decorations, Njegos 1st order and Njegos 2nd order, and I also have some other tokens of recognition, if you will. I did not mention that the municipality also commended me for taking certain measures in the municipality during the war to preserve peace.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Not taking certain measures to preserve peace, but to preserve peace; right?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MILINCIC
utterances.text: Yes, and to develop the municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell us what the ethnic composition was of your municipality in 1990 and 1991?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MILINCIC
utterances.text: Identical, like today and before 1990 -- actually, from 1948 onwards, the first elections held after that war. 91 to 95 per cent of the Serb municipality and the population is 21.800-something. This last sentence showed that the number is a bit less, about 19.000. So the ethnic composition of the municipality of Srbac is 95 per cent Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This decrease, in proportional terms, how is that reflected in terms of the ethnic communities?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MILINCIC
utterances.text: I understand what you're saying. In terms of percentage, Serbs, Muslims, Croats, Ruthenians, Czechs, there was a proportional decrease, about a thousand inhabitants less than ten years ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you please tell us what the name Srbac means and whether we changed it during the war, or rather, when was this name established?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MILINCIC
utterances.text: Yes, there was some prejudice there and some malicious interpretations in terms of the name Srbac. I think that some connotations came even from here, that Srbac is a new municipality. No. Sometime in November, I think, 1933, that is to say, during the Kingdom of Yugoslavia, the minister of the interior of the Kingdom of Yugoslavia made a decision that Bosanski Svinjar -- there were two Svinjars, now there is a new one, Davor. So Bosnian Svinjar was supposed to be renamed Srbac in 1933.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you just tell the Trial Chamber what that means, the name of the town?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MILINCIC
utterances.text: There are three versions why, in 1933, this name was inaugurated. The Sava River meanders nearby in the shape of a scythe, so that is what people thought it meant, but no. Also it is the Serbs, the ethnic composition there, and then Serbs, Srbac, so that that led to the name of Srbac.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I hope that the transcript, when they listen to all of this, they're going to put the right names there. All right. Can you tell us in terms of politics, which political party did you join in 1990 and why, what led you to join that party?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MILINCIC
utterances.text: Well, yes. I worked as a professor in a secondary school. I taught my students, I taught them literature and language. I have to say that there were quite a few students from Croatia, from Davor, who crossed the Sava River in boats in order to attend school. And then when these things happened, when multi-national states started disintegrating, the Soviet Union, Czechoslovakia, as I followed Dedijer's book, his book called "A Contribution to the Biography of Josip Broz Tito," I thought that it was time to identify ourselves culturally, linguistically and ethnically, quite simply that we should not be ashamed and that we should not be afraid of acknowledging this co-existence. I thought it was time to affirm that which is good for all the ethnic communities. In that other war in 1941, 1945, in the Srbac municipality, there were never any conflicts, especially not with the Croats. And I thought that as a humanist I could contribute to the affirmation of all to a maximum degree. It was it. Maybe this was a rather romantic credo that I could help the development of democracy in that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. When did you establish that political party and did I attend that gathering?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MILINCIC
utterances.text: Yes, on the 28th of July, in Srbac, we had an initiative committee. I happened to be there -- well, I'm not saying by accident, but I wanted to observe things and see how things would develop. And our priest suggested that I be a member of this initiative committee, and then people thought: Well, a humanist, a literate man, not encumbered by this or that, and in that kind of environment, that kind of man was needed. And that's how it started. You know, as they say, it's hard for people to let you go once you've joined in. And then I went around, making speeches, and then this ceremony took place in Srbac on the 31st of August, 1990. On the square in Srbac -- well, the journalists estimated that there were about 10.000 people there. The population of the town of Srbac is 6.000 otherwise. So there were about 10.000 people there. I spoke there, you spoke there, Vojo Kupresanin spoke there, Zlatko Kelecevic, and we said what the objective was, what the programme of the party was, ecology, to conserve the environment, also to develop these relations of partnership. I can say that you got quite a bit of applause and I think that I provided that by way of evidence. I think that you really won over the audience with a single sentence. Can I say what that was?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MILOS MILINCIC
utterances.text: That went on for about two hours and then you spoke and you said that it is being held against us, the Serb Democratic Party, that we were too peaceful. And you quoted a folk epic about Marko Kraljevic and his mother because he was behaving in strange way, carrying his spear the other way around, and he said: If we run into trouble, I can turn the spear. And you said that's what we're going to do. And then the key sentence that won over the audience, these were ovations: Some adventures are advocating peace -- advocating war --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- but they did not ask Serb mothers whether they had children to send to war. A garden is most beautiful when it is multi-coloured, so do your best in order to have your neighbours live in safety and security so that they do not feel squeezed in as a minority. That was truly welcomed. I have to say that this campaign was ideological rather than ethnic. How do I put this? It was a sort of competition between the former communists and the new national parties. So it was a clash between the right wing and the left wing. On ethnic grounds, nobody would have won any votes in Srbac if they said anything bad about Serbs, about Croats, about Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can the witness be shown 1D15612.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: We'll show a video-clip that you announced a moment ago.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 1D15612. It should be played from 11.15.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us what we are looking at?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MILINCIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's that famous rally. It was already dusk.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we rewind to the beginning and turn the volume up. The interpreters have a transcript.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that's the applause I mentioned.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "Our enemies are not only those who hate the Serbs. Our enemies are those who are against democracy, and I can tell you that democracy is threatened these days. It's threatened not only by those who had been in power until now but" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Why don't we upload the transcript, English and B/C/S, and then -- unless there's a -- unless Mr. Tieger opposes to that idea. I don't think there's a point reviewing this image at this condition right now.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Sorry, Mr. President. No, of course I have no objection to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Shall we switch to e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: It should be page 2.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we show the second page with a passage that begins at 11.15. If the parties agree, we can tender the entire transcript, of course, but I would like this shown in the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you introduce this part of the speech, Professor Milincic?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MILINCIC
utterances.text: You concluded that popular gathering and people had perhaps expected some very rigid positions from you, but after you said that democracy was threatened on many levels, that many people, some people at least of adventurous vent who were advocating war, obviously had not asked Muslims, Serb, and Croat mothers whether they were prepared to sacrifice their children for war. And when you said that good neighbourly relations should be fostered, and then came that sentence that I already mentioned, the beautiful sentence, that a garden is most beautiful when it is full of flowers of different colours, and in the same way, people live the best when they are prepared to live together in harmony and in peace.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I tender these two pages, with your leave, Your Honours, and the recording.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Do we see a passage relating to garden here?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It could be on the first page or perhaps it was said in my conversations with political representatives --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Wait, wait, wait, wait.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Sorry, there's no point in warning Dr. Karadzic repeatedly --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: -- but that's another example.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: During the course of proofing you heard this video-clip, the audio part of this video, didn't you? Mr. Karadzic's speech at that rally?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I participated in the rally just like Mr. Karadzic, and I have at home the full recording.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Excellencies, on page 1 in the passage that begins with 04.59, the last two sentences, it is not a reference to a garden specifically, but it mentions flourishing --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: This --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It may not have be a garden or perhaps a meadow --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: You need to put that to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I mean, it's -- now we're having the form of Dr. Karadzic testifying and asking the witness to confirm his testimony. It's a continuing pattern.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I apologise. That's not the way it is. We are just looking for this in the transcript. I'm asking the witness to look at the last -- the penultimate paragraph, in fact, where it says: "The Serbian nation in Bosnia-Herzegovina could have organised themselves into some grumpy and dangerous organisation ..."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] "The Serbian nation in Bosnia-Herzegovina could have organised themselves into some pugnacious and dangerous organisation, but it did not because Serbian people are loyal to democracy. Whenever there was democracy, the Serbian people flourished. Of course, other nations flourished as well. It will be like that again, if there is democracy and civil peace." These are the words that persuaded me to be a member of the party and one of the leaders of the party, these words precisely. That's how I understood democracy and our abilities to live in one state with other nations.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can I ask you to pay attention to the passage that begins with 3.26, what am I talking about there?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MILINCIC
utterances.text: It says: "I have to say, the authorities did ask that from other nations as well. We, the Serbs, did not destroy the monument of Ban Jelacic in Zagreb, the authorities did that. We do not have any problem with the monument. They can set it up again if they need it. It was not we, Serbs, that looked with animosity to our Muslim neighbours when they celebrated Bajram. On the contrary, we congratulated them on that holiday. It was not we that prevented their shrines in Hajvatovica and Devojacka Pecina. We will respect their sanctuaries and visit them as the Muslims respect our monastery Ostrog and visit it. That is the way one lives in a community and municipality. There is no reason for anyone to give up anything. Therefore, we seek to restore everything that makes us a nation: Our history, our religion, and our customs. We ask the same for our neighbours, Croats, Muslims, Jews, Romas, and others. We will not love them more if they give up on themselves. Let them live with their full spiritual being. That way they will be more peaceful as well and they will be better neighbours to us." This is required reading for democracy. I, as a teacher of literature, realised that this was a dream one should aspire to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We will admit this -- Mr. Karadzic's speech at the rally.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It receives Exhibit Number D4185, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Were you an official of the Serbian Democratic Party; where and in which period?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MILINCIC
utterances.text: From 28th July 1990 until year 2002, I was all the time on various bodies for the Serbian Democratic Party, beginning as president of the Municipal Board of the party in Srbac, and then three terms of office as the member of the republic organisation of the party.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You were on the Main Board three times. How were you elected?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MILINCIC
utterances.text: I was nominated by my party unit in Srbac, and then proposals came from all municipalities. And by secret ballot, because there were a number of candidates on the ticket, I received - let me not say the majority - but a very large number of votes. I don't know why, is it my personal charm or is it because I'm a teacher of literature, but in any case I was elected.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you take part in charting the policies and the political positions of the party during those three terms of office?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MILINCIC
utterances.text: Yes, one can say that all the time in that period I was in a position where I could follow the work of the party and convey the positions of the party to my own municipal unit. And when the war had already started, when we had no more electricity, when we were left to our own devices, your positions and what I learned from you helped me to be a good leader.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What's missing from the transcript is that: When we had no more electricity or communications. Could you speak more slowly, please. While you participated in charting the policies of the Serbian Democratic Party, did the party ever depart from what you heard at that rally and what attracted you initially to the party?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MILINCIC
utterances.text: I already told you about what motivated me to become a member of that party. And then the party platform, as I was studying some materials and looking back at my own diaries and agendas, even in 1990, before the elections, we said that we would be co-operating with all the other parties, on the condition that they don't have the four antis in their programmes. And that is anti-democracy, anti-Semitism, anti-Serbdom --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter missed the fourth one.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That means --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could you repeat from the fourth one, fourth anti.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We said that after the elections we would co-operate and make coalitions with all the parties - Srbac had five of them at the elections - and we conveyed that to the Main Board as our position. We would co-operate with all the parties that don't have four antis - anti-democracy, anti-Semitism, anti-Serbdom, and anti-Yugoslavdom - in their programme. We thought that we would be developing Yugoslavia in the spirit of tolerance, unity, and community. Unfortunately, it didn't turn out that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Who in your municipality was the most important personality in power who put into practice the policies of the Serbian Democratic Party?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MILINCIC
utterances.text: When we were cut off, when we lost communications, when we didn't see each other or heard from each other so often anymore, I was at the head of the party, rallying people around me, guiding them to look for a modus vivendi, first as the president of the party and then president of the Municipal Assembly of Srbac for seven years. I was the one who got all the praise and all the criticism and I survived.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In your work in the authorities in Srbac, did you apply to the greatest possible extent the policies of the Serbian Democratic Party?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MILINCIC
