utterances.text: Once we had won the elections, when the Municipal Assembly of Srbac numbered 60 deputies, from five political parties, the Serbian Democratic Party had won 42 seats out of 60; the Socialist Party, eight; the reformists, six; the SPO, two. I think that adds up. Then when we were forming the government, since there was a -- there were some misgivings towards other ideologies, and I was thinking of you when you said that we would do very wisely in Srbac if -- with regard to the party of SDA that had only two seats, it would be very fair, and you even called me to tell me that: Why don't you give an important position to the SDA, a position of authority? I consulted with my associates, with my co-workers, and there were some frictions, but since there will be weddings among the Muslim communities it would be good to put one of them from the SDA, the registrar's office, to give them the position of vice-president even. So that's how Halid Hadziselimovic became my deputy.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You've just told us that the structure of the population was the same before the war and after the war. Where did Muslims in Srbac live in terms of the urban nucleus and were there any Muslim neighbourhoods on the outskirts of Srbac?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MILINCIC
utterances.text: Yes, Kobas along the Sava. There was our own Serbian Kobas, Bosnian Kobas, and there is a Croatian Kobas across the river Sava. In our Serbian Kobas about 80 families lived there from the beginning of times, as it were. On one occasion you passed through there as a young man, you told me about that. You passed through Crna and you wanted to know whether there were such people there. Some 50 families live in Crna. And in the town of Srbac itself, there is a certain number of Muslim families as well. In other words, Muslim families mostly lived in Kobas, in Crna, and in Srbac of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you, and to what extent, respect their needs, their rights? Did you take into account all of their demands and requests? I'm talking about the pre-war period.

utterances.speaker: MILOS MILINCIC
utterances.text: The principal of the school in Kobas - and let me tell you that the Kobas school is a branch of the Srbac school - his name was Rasin Zukanovic. He was the principal of that school, for a very good reason. Later on, we changed the name of that school in Kobas and we named it Mehmed Mesa Selimovic instead of a Second World War -- the central school in Srbac in Jovan Jovanovic Zmaj and the branch school in Kobas was named Mehmed Mesa Selimovic, who was a great writer and author.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In that respect, did you know what my position was and did we talk about that on any occasion?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MILINCIC
utterances.text: On one occasion you told me something that surprised me. You always wondered whether there were pressures and problems and how people there behaved, and then I answered: Well, there are problems everywhere, aren't there? For some people --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Please slow down. Your previous answer was totally mis-recorded. Can you please slow down.

utterances.speaker: MILOS MILINCIC
utterances.text: When you question me about the situation in the municipality and whether there were any pressures put to bear on those people, because there was a war going on, then I told you that there are problems everywhere. Of course there are mobsters, scavengers of all sorts who do all sorts of things when the night falls. And then you said: Let alone those scaven gers and mobsters. What about Muslims, Ruthenians, Croats and others in Srbac? And I said: Well, we're trying to protect them. And then at one point you got bored with my answers and you told me: Milos, if you in Srbac are afraid and if you are bothered by the less than 1.000 non-Serbs, then you're not Serbs. You're not even humans. And then you used an expression that really surprised me and I can't repeat it here.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Why not? Repeat it.

utterances.speaker: MILOS MILINCIC
utterances.text: And then you said: There are 22.000 inhabitants in Srbac and there is less than 1.000 non-Serbs, and if you are bothered by them, like some are, then you are neither humans nor Serbs, you are mere cunts. I really -- I was taken by surprise with your answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I myself was really taken by surprise when I realised how many swearwords I used in telephone conversations, but I'm also taken by surprise by today's transcript. I suppose this will be reviewed and corrected.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Can Mr. Karadzic repeat the document number.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And while we are waiting for the document, can you please explain what was the misunderstanding involving the school in Kobas?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: If Dr. Karadzic is surprised by the transcript, it may in part be because one can hear the interpreter racing to keep up, breathlessly. So it's not only the witness who is apparently speaking too fast, but in trying to keep up with Mr. Karadzic's speed, you can hear the strain in her voice and the pace of her translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Tieger. Do you remember the question, Mr. Milincic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You have to repeat it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let me just call up 65 ter 31802 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Before calling up the document, can you not ask a question to the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. President, I think the document is the intercept of the conversation that they've just been discussing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Oh, very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Oh, yes. It was not very clear when you spoke about the school in Kobas. What was the problem with its name?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MILINCIC
utterances.text: I believe that it's name was Esad Midzic, and then names were being changed, other names were given to those schools to deal with the ideological rifts because those ideological divisions were already --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Before we go on, we had -- we need to find out who these interlocutors are first of all.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I thought that you can read it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you identify this document? Who are the interlocutors?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MILINCIC
utterances.text: The two of us, President Karadzic and Milos Milincic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: When --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The document says "Milos Milosic," no reference to Mr. Milincic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes, this is a mistake. Milos Milincic. This is me. There is no two ways about it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: How do you know this is a mistake? You have to establish that it was the witness, Mr. Karadzic, first of all.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Milincic, could you please tell us where it says "Srbac municipality ... Municipal Assembly chairman Milos Milosic needs you ..." was there a Milos Milosic?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MILINCIC
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Was this mis-recorded by the person who was listening in?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MILINCIC
utterances.text: At that time I was the Municipal Assembly chairman and my name is Milos Milincic, so this is a mistake.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excellencies, we have the audio. It's of poor quality. However, the voices may be recognised and identified.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And the context is rather self-explanatory.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Now I'm fine. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. We can read this. I'd like us to look at the following page.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Could you please tell us what this is all about.

utterances.speaker: MILOS MILINCIC
utterances.text: Yes, the school in Kobas, I believe it bore the name of a war hero from the Second World War, Esad Midzic. We wanted to put that into a different frame, an artistic frame. So there was a discussion as to what name to give to the school in Kobas. There was some extreme demands, one of them was for the school to be named Saint Sava, and the two MPs from the SDA reacted. They were against it. They didn't want the name to be Saint Sava because they were Bosniaks, Muslims, and there are some associations with that name. There were some problems with that. And then another proposal was Ducic and then Njegos. But Njegos was the name already given to another school. There were some comical situations with this regard. And then you either called me or I called you. I called you to consult you, whether I should embark on that at all or whether to put it on hold or whether we should be somewhat faster and harsher in all of that. And then you have -- had some proposals, and then you said: Be smart and look for a compromise. Jovan Ducic, or if that is not doable then you proposed something else that was quite endearing. You said if you had to guard the name of the school with police forces, then there is something wrong with that name obviously.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we look at the following English page.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you remember what my comment was on the name of Saint Sava, whether I said that it was their heritage as well?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MILINCIC
utterances.text: Yes, we tried to discuss to those -- to discuss matters with those two MPs, we wanted to impart on them that Saint Sava was an enlightener, that he was popular even before the last war, that schools had reviews to celebrate Saint Sava, that one shouldn't be narrow-minded because Saint Sava was a do-gooder, he was an educator, and that he was accepted by everybody as an exceptional figure, a figure in the world of culture. But people didn't know that, that's why they reacted spontaneously. I know that one of my own MPs who was a Serb, he said: Leave aside Saint Sava. What book did he author? And I told him what canons Saint Sava authored, but we left it at that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can I please ask you to tell us, in our conversation a mention was made of some things. What was my recommendation? What direction should you seek to reach a compromise?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MILINCIC
utterances.text: Your proposal was Vuk Karadzic. I said: No, we can't do that because we have already given that name to another school. What about Jovan Ducic, you said? The socialists started looking for his ideological flaws. They said that Ducic was a Chetnik who emigrated to America, so we wanted to deal with that as well. And then you said: Okay, what about Mehmed Mesa Selimovic, maybe that's not bad. You actually left it to me. You told me you seek my advice but it's up to you to deal with that. But I wanted to consult you, I didn't want to rush into things. I received a letter from Ostoja, I have it here with me. People from Ostoja wrote to me because they were dissatisfied with all the changes of the names of schools.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. What about the central school in Srbac, what was its name and what about the branch in Kobas?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MILINCIC
utterances.text: In Srbac it was Jovan Jovanovic Zmaj, who was a very well-known children's author loved by everybody across the board because he wrote warmly about children, without any differences, without any ideology. And as for the school in Kobas was named after another great author, Mehmed Mesa Selimovic. That was the compromise.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. During the war, did you have an occasion to preserve your minorities and how did you do that?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MILINCIC
utterances.text: I have to say this: There was scavengers, as I've already told you, who benefitted from night-time and they wore arms in Lepenica Srbac. The family Malesevic were killed. Three perpetrators were arrested. They were Serbs, one committed suicide and the other two were sentenced to death. However, they were -- their sentence was changed to 20 years' imprisonment. In Razbor, which is another place, the Vejinovic family was attacked. They were looking for money and fuel. They were beaten and mutilated. In a village called Kladanj, a shop was robbed and the Serbs beat up the owner. There was a lot of fear of Muslims. The fact was that we set up a police check-point in Kobas to protect people in Kobas from the -- from the incursions, from those huge national heros who were actually robbers and plunderers, nothing else.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you please tell us who were the victims, what was their ethnicity? For example, the Malesevics, the Vejinovics, who were they and who were the perpetrators of those crimes?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MILINCIC
utterances.text: The Malesevic family was --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Speak slowly and put a pause. Yes, please continue. Repeat your -- the answer, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Malesevic family in Gornja Lepenica, they were a married couple who were retired after having worked in Germany all their lives. They were riched [as interpreted]. They were killed by three Serbs. They were arrested. They were the perpetrators of that crime. They were sentenced to death. One of them committed suicide. And the other two had their sentences changed to 20 years' imprisonment. As for the Vejinovic's in Razbor, we never established -- the police did not have enough proof. Some Serbs were brought in for questioning. In Kladari, which was a Serbian settlement, people don't dare testify, they don't dare say anything. However, some scavengers came there, they were also Serbs. Why am I saying all this? Because I was held at gunpoint. Some soldiers held me at gunpoint, they were Serbs. The situation was really bad and ugly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you please help us, were there any instances of emigration of minority members from your municipality? How did Muslim able-bodied men as well as Croatian able-bodied men behave?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MILINCIC
utterances.text: The companies didn't operate. The situation persisted for a long time. There was no communication with the world. There was nothing to live on. We can talk about the emigration of Serbs from Davor, which was on the border. In any case, I was informed about some 60 Bosniak Muslims, not families, but individuals, especially younger individuals, who emigrated to third countries because they didn't have jobs. Their assets, their property, was protected. Serbs did move into some of their houses. They were refugees in Srbac from various territories of the former Bosnia and Herzegovina. When the war was over, the property was returned to their original owners.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. What about a majority of the people, save for those 60 individuals, did they remain living in Srbac?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MILINCIC
utterances.text: No, there was no exodus at all. And when you asked me about fighters or the troops, I have to tell you I have some materials in my briefcase. 22 Muslims fought in the Srbac Brigade. They were wounded and they have received decisions, based on which they now enjoy benefits as war veterans and invalids. 22 Muslim fighters were wounded in the Srbac Brigade. Many of them were outside of the Srbac Brigade. There was a burial that I attended when a soldier, a Muslim soldier, had been killed. I made sure that hodza attended and performed religious rites. It's easy to talk about that now, but one had to have guts to do that, to bring a hodza. I had problems because of that, people held it against me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Let's clarify one thing. You didn't mention the word "exodus." You said that there was no moving out.

utterances.speaker: MILOS MILINCIC
utterances.text: No, no, no. There was no exodus. People did not leave.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: When you said that people were outside of the Srbac Brigade, what did you mean by that? That they were in other units?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MILINCIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, a majority were in the Srbac Brigade, but they were also in the 16th and other units.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you now tell us whether in your vicinity there were other municipalities where the presidents of the municipalities managed to preserve peace for their minorities? Who were the presidents of those municipalities and what was their relationship with the Main Board?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MILINCIC
utterances.text: If I were to recapitulate after all of this, the top people of the party and of the municipality, again I don't know whether it depended on ability and communication and then the programme of the party itself. These municipalities resisted the war to quite an extent. For example, Srbac, the Srbac municipality, I was president of the municipality and the Main Board. That was considered to be the safest municipality throughout the war. We can discuss that a bit more later on. Then there was Gradiska, that municipality, where the percentage of Bosniaks, Muslims, was greater than in Srbac. There were certain municipalities there, but somehow the balance was preserved. Prnjavor, that municipality too. They used to call Prnjavor a small-scale Yugoslavia because there were several ethnic communities. Now, if I were to recapitulate, perhaps this is a clash of interests from this point of view, but then there was this concentration of power to keep it as simple as possible and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Who were the presidents of municipalities? You mentioned Gradiska, Prnjavor, Laktasi, Mrkonjic Grad --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Did he say Laktasi?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: No --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no, I'm just adding now these municipalities and I want to ask who the presidents of those municipalities were.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Candidates of the Serb Democratic Party, Nebojsa Ivastanin, president of the SDS in Gradiska; Stevan Jovic, also a member of the SDS, president of the SDS in Laktasi, that's where Premier Dodik is from, or rather, he's now the president of the Republika Srpska; in Mrkonjic, Dr. Luka Cudic, I think that was his name; in Prnjavor, the candidate of the SDS Nemanja Vasic. And let me not enumerate all of it. Trebinje --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you, thank you. What was the position of these presidents in relation to the Main Board?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MILINCIC
utterances.text: We met often, we communicated. If somebody did not attend a Main Board meeting for any reason, then those who did go would convey what happened there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Were they members of the Main Board?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MILINCIC
utterances.text: Nebojsa, president of Gradiska, was; Nemanja Vasic was; Stevan Jovic, I think he wasn't a member of the Main Board; Luka Cudic in Mrkonjic, he was; Bozidar Vucurevic in Trebinje, he was. Now I cannot remember anymore. I think that these people who took it upon themselves to indeed be the most responsible persons and that's where there was the least number of problems.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Milincic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excellencies, I have no further questions at this point. Could this intercept please be admitted all together with the audio recording.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Any objection, Mr. Tieger?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: No, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Do we need to admit the audio?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We don't have to, but if somebody's interested.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. We'll receive this intercept.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It receives Exhibit Number D4186, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Milincic, this is not the first time that you've testified before this Tribunal. You also testified in the Krajisnik case as a Defence witness in November of 2005; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MILINCIC
utterances.text: That's right, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And you also gave a statement to the Karadzic Defence in connection with this particular case, which I imagine happened sometime this year; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MILINCIC
utterances.text: Yes, sometime in July or August, I think it was August.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, Dr. Karadzic asked you at page 46 whether the party had departed from what was said at the rally in September of 1990, that we looked at during your examination-in-chief and reviewed the transcript. Now, those statements at the time from Dr. Karadzic which you indicated the party did not depart from would then have included --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And I guess we need to call up D4185, the transcript of that rally and Dr. Karadzic's speech.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: It would have included, for example, in the portion that appears under 4.59, at approximately the fourth sentence there, the statement: "You would like to live in peace with others but the others must have the same measure of this desire in order to live together. Serbs, you will treat others strictly in the way the others treat you, no more, no less ..." So that was one of the statements made by Dr. Karadzic at the time; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MILINCIC
utterances.text: Mm-hm.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And at 6.55, at the end of that portion, he also stated: "We will not take anything what belongs to others and we will not leave anything that belongs to us ..." And that was part of what Dr. Karadzic stated in September of 1990 that you indicated the party didn't later depart from; right?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Next page in Serbian, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I just wanted you to confirm that. Or are you able to find that? It should be just at the end of that portion, it's a very small portion.

utterances.speaker: MILOS MILINCIC
utterances.text: Are you referring to 11.15: "But our enemies are not only those who hate Serbs ..." Is that what you had in mind?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: No, I said at the end of 6.55: "We will not take anything what belongs to others and we will not leave anything that belongs to us ..." So that's correct also; right?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MILINCIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And although it's not included in this portion of the speech that was transcribed by the Defence, you yourself alluded to a reference to Marko Kraljevic and the image of him carrying the spear the other way around until such time as he needed it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And if we could upload 65 ter 40635A, have a transcript of what I believe to be that portion.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: That appears -- that appears at -- another upload that was double-checked if I'm not mistaken, essentially the same translation but let's make sure. In any event, the B/C/S is the same as you see here. I'm going to read the English portion of the translation that we received. It is indeed a reference to the Marko Kraljevic image that you quoted. It appears at 1.17.22 through 1.17.48 of the rally. And it says basically: We shall not be harsh also on account of that old poem about Marko Kraljevic when he carried the spear upside down and the fairy warns him not to carry it upside down or that way and Marko replies: I shall easily bring about the spear should trouble beset me. That's a quote from Marko. And then Dr. Karadzic continues: We shall be benign and democratic right up to the moment until democracy is no longer able to function. And then when someone -- at the moment when someone attacks us, we shall bring about the spear. So that's another reflection, according to you, as I understand it, in the -- of what was said or conveyed by Dr. Karadzic at the rally and from which the party did not depart when the time came?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MILINCIC
utterances.text: I have to tell you that the people, especially the Serb people, bearing in mind their legacy, the fear that was instilled in them decades before that --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Milincic --

utterances.speaker: MILOS MILINCIC
utterances.text: -- we embarked upon the development of democracy and -- yes?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Excuse me, sir. I have a limited period of time. I think you answered Dr. Karadzic's questions. I ask you to answer mine. And my question was whether or not this is indeed what Dr. Karadzic said at the rally and which you indicated were matters that the party did not later depart from. Is that correct or not?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MILINCIC
utterances.text: We did not depart from democracy. If we are attacked, then we have to defend ourselves. That is the applause that was received from everyone at the rally. If we were attacked, and we weren't expected to be attacked.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: You asked a compound question. Do you confirm Mr. Karadzic said that at the time, at that rally?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That was said and everyone understands that properly. I don't see what it is that is problematic here.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: So I tender that, Mr. President, to be added to the previous exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I'm not sure how we can add that video --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: That's true. Okay. Well, let's just have it as a supplemental exhibit and we can link it -- I understand the Registrar --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Is it possible to add this part, technically? I'm just asking.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Do you want it added to the video as well as the transcript?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yeah, if we are to add it, it should be added that way. We'll admit it separately.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: I think that would be easier.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. As a Prosecution exhibit.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It receives Exhibit P6563, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I hope there's some cross-reference between these two -- each other --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: In other contexts I'm told the Registrar can do that. Mr. President, I'm about to move on to another matter. I don't think we could get too deeply into it before we would break, so perhaps it's best to adjourn at this point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. We'll have a break for 45 minutes and resume at quarter past 1.00. --- Luncheon recess taken at 12.28 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Milincic, at about page 54 of today's transcript you mentioned some crimes in Srbac and alluded to at least one prosecution. The last time you were here and testified in the Krajisnik case, you also raised the issue of crimes and prosecutions. And in particular, you brought to the Court's attention the killing of Mr. Hadziselimovic, who you mentioned today, in order to show the Court that a prominent Muslim had been murdered and the authorities responded by prosecuting and imprisoning the perpetrator. Correct? That's what happened the last time you were here.

utterances.speaker: MILOS MILINCIC
utterances.text: Hadziselimovic was my vice-president, but at the time when this incident occurred in this restaurant with one or more protagonists, he was -- he had deregistered --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Sorry, Mr. Milincic --

utterances.speaker: MILOS MILINCIC
utterances.text: -- because he had an apartment --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: -- I'm not asking for you to recap the entirety of the Hadziselimovic murder. I'm asking you whether or not it's true - and I can show you and will show you if necessary the transcript of your testimony in the Krajisnik case - that you came to the Court and you asserted that Mr. Hadziselimovic had been murdered by Mr. Stankovic and that Mr. Stankovic had been prosecuted for that murder?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MILINCIC
utterances.text: It is correct that that happened. Mr. Stankovic was convicted because of some other crimes or misdemeanours in addition to this murder, but this killing of Hadziselimovic was a fight. I checked that later on after my testimony here. It happened in a brawl. I did not have information, the right kind of information then. The fact is that Hadziselimovic as he was passing by this tavern, he reacted to a song, and then there was this brawl and he died in hospital in Banja Luka five or six days later. Hadziselimovic, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Let's try to get the chronology of your information and the provision of the type of information that you wanted to convey to the Court correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: So if we could turn to 65 ter 25768, page -- well, let's get that first and then I can turn you -- direct you to the page. Too many numbers. Okay. And turn, please, to page 18450.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Give me this in my language.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I'll have to read it to you and it will be translated, sir, but I hope that your recollection of the event will be refreshed by the portions that are read back to you verbatim.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: 18450, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Here I was recapping for you what you had stated in your examination-in-chief to the Court, and I stated to you that: "... what you wanted to show the Court was that in that instance in particular, a prominent and well-regarded Muslim had been murdered and the Serbian authorities had responded by prosecuting and imprisoning the perpetrator for that; correct?" And your answer was: "Yes." So that's the first thing, Mr. Milincic. It's true that you brought the Court's attention to this event in order to show how rigorous the reaction by the Serbian authorities was; right?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MILINCIC
utterances.text: That's how you interpret it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: No, Mr. Milincic --

utterances.speaker: MILOS MILINCIC
utterances.text: At that point --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Excuse me, sir. I just read -- do you dispute what you said here? The question was: You wanted to show the Court that in that instance a prominent and well-regarded Muslim had been murdered and the Serbian authorities responded by prosecuting and imprisoning the perpetrator for that; correct? Your answer was "yes" in 2005. Do you deny that?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MILINCIC
utterances.text: I'm not denying that that's what I said, but when I checked later it wasn't a murder, it was a brawl in a tavern and the man died in hospital five or six days later. I as president of the municipality did not have to know about all of these details, just like I don't know all the details concerning the killing of the Malesevic family.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I see. So your explanation to the Court on this occasion is that when Mr. Hadziselimovic, a prominent and well-regarded Muslim in your community who was your deputy was killed and a man was arrested for his murder and you say imprisoned and prosecuted, now you say that was simply a brawl; is that it? So you didn't know about that at the time. You only found out about what happened to Mr. Hadziselimovic long afterwards. That's your explanation?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MILINCIC
utterances.text: My explanation was that that happened, that there was a brawl, that a man died in hospital, that the military authorities arrested the mentioned gentleman, they interrogated him and released him after a while, and then in the meantime he did other things. That is the truth and that is undeniable. Perhaps I rushed on and said that he was sentenced immediately. No. He was interviewed, released, allowed to go home, and then in the meantime he committed some other crimes and was then convicted. That is the full truth.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: The fact of the matter is that the Trial Chamber in the Krajisnik case looked at the documents you brought to establish your claim that Mr. Stankovic had been prosecuted and imprisoned for the Hadziselimovic murder and asked you -- well, let me read this to you. "Q. And with respect to the documents you brought with you" -- this is the bottom of page 18450 going on to 18451. "Q. With respect to the documents you brought with you concerning the murder of Mr. Hadziselimovic, the Court in particular asked you how it could know which murder these documents referred to, because it didn't seem clear on its face, and you assured the Court that it referred to the murder of Mr. Hadziselimovic because you knew how important it was to be accurate here and bring accurate information to the Court; is that right?" And your answer was: "A. Yes." That's what you said in 2005; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MILINCIC
utterances.text: I have to intervene. When you drew my attention to this, the sequence of events, what happened to Stankovic or Hadziselimovic, then I saw that I was not fully aware of all the details. And then I said you're right. Check that. That's what I said -- oh, then you're right. It was an oversight on my part with regard to some things, I mean in terms of time an oversight. Now it is a fact that this man was sentenced to six years in prison for what he did, but after the brawl with Hadziselimovic, the military authorities, the court, released him. There was a war going on and they had no place to keep all these people in detention. And then when he did other things, then he was arrested, prosecuted, and convicted to six years in prison. And that is the full truth and that can be checked. I as president of the municipality, I wanted to say that no one was coddled, if you will. Serbs or Muslims, or anybody. And if bad things happen on one side, of course they would happen on the other side too.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And I tender 18450 and 51, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. We'll receive it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It receives Exhibit Number P6564, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Milincic, you've alluded a couple of times to what happened after that so let me quickly recap the Stankovic affair. First of all, in May of 1992 -- and now if we could turn to 18465, track what you confirmed in 2005. All right. Looking back -- looking down to the bottom third of the page: In May of 1992, Mr. Stankovic murdered Mr. Hadziselimovic. In August of 1992, he murdered Hasima Zukanovic, a woman, and Reuf Alagic, and shot and seriously injured Hamza Bojadzic and Sabra Alagic, Mr. Alagic's mother. And then having been released again, in September of 1994, he shot two Serb children and then was finally, at that point, put in prison until approximately 2002. That's all correct; right? And you confirmed on the top of the next page: "It is correct what you have just said." That was your testimony in 2005; right?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Why don't you read out the full sentence.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: His answer --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: The question was: "That's all correct; right?" Your answer was: "Now you have just reminded me of the Serbian children. I have completely forgotten about them, unfortunately. It is correct what you have just said. That detail, unfortunately, has escaped me." That was your testimony in 2005; right? About the chain of events with respect to Mr. Stankovic?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: We don't see the proper --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know where the misunderstanding is. I only assisted you to get the right chronology, which I initially overlooked. Now, why he was convicted -- sentenced to six years, why he had been released early, I don't know. It was up to the military authorities. I was not hiding anything and I'm not hiding anything now. I'm sorry for everybody who fell victim, for the Muslims and for the Malesevics. Those are crazy things in war. You can't control them.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I tender those two pages, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we'll add them.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: You also responded to some questions today from Mr. Karadzic about other municipalities and other presidents of municipalities and so on. And I'll get to that in a moment, but I note that the -- I asked you earlier about both your testimony and your statement. And I note, for example, that the subject of the rally and the speech that you discussed with Dr. Karadzic earlier was covered in the statement you provided to the Karadzic Defence; correct? You addressed that topic in your statement; right?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MILINCIC
utterances.text: Yes, what I wrote and what I stated. We're talking now. Where is the problem?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Can we call up 1D09746, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Can I ask you to just take a quick look at this and you can look through as many of the pages as you wish and confirm that this is the statement you gave the Karadzic Defence in approximately July of this year?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MILINCIC
utterances.text: What am I supposed to do, confirm this?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: No, just confirm whether or not that is the statement that you gave the Karadzic Defence. I'll ask you about -- I may or may not ask you about some of the details.

utterances.speaker: MILOS MILINCIC
utterances.text: The statement is authentic and I stand by it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Now, in -- when this statement was assembled, how was that done? Did the Karadzic -- the representative or representatives of the Karadzic Defence team suggest to you the issues that should be covered?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. President, just as a -- I don't have an objection, but I want to note that if this question is answered, we would be tendering the statement. We think the statement would be relevant at this point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, I think the Court will have to wait and see whether the contents of the statement are or are not relevant for purposes of admission. But the mere fact that I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Given that he testified viva voce, why don't you put your question directly and then see how it is reflected in the statement. And then you can ask that question.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I would appreciate the opportunity to ask a couple of preliminary questions, Mr. President, though.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Because, as you will see, the question I ultimately ask may implicate the understanding of how that was prepared.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: So just a couple of questions --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. This is the pause you should put. Yes, please go on.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Are these -- in essence, are these all your words or did the Karadzic Defence team suggest to you what you should say in the statement?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. President, I do object now because if you -- if we're talking about the substance of the statement and how it was taken as opposed to something that is inconsistent with his testimony, then I think that the statement itself would have to be admitted. Since you've denied the admission of the statement under 92 ter, now I think that the Prosecution is required -- is giving grounds for the statement to be admitted. It would be unfair to discuss how the statement was prepared without admitting its entire contents. So that's my point.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Those are total apples and oranges, Mr. President. And I will turn to a specific portion of the statement that will make these questions relevant, I can assure you. I don't intend to ask these totally in the abstract --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: -- but the mere fact --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just -- just a second.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And we'll consider whether it's necessary to admit this document -- statement later on.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Milincic, do you recall the question I asked before the intervention, that was: Are these all your words or did the Karadzic Defence team suggest to you what you should say in the statement?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MILINCIC
utterances.text: I'm a man in good health who raised generations, interpreted visionary, artistic messages, and I don't need dictation. I spoke, and as I -- I said as a president of the municipality I did this, this, this, and that, item by item, which I described here. Whether it's a coincidence that the representative of the Defence wanted me to talk about certain things and I already knew what I needed to say, how the party was established, why the war started, what Karadzic told us, what he suggested to the municipalities because municipalities were states on a small scale. And in all my contacts and situations, I couldn't wait for Karadzic, I had to deal with problems myself. So this question, whether something was suggested to me, is superfluous.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please be asked to slow down.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Milincic, you spoke a bit too fast. Please repeat from your -- where -- from where you said something suggested was superfluous.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise. The statement that I gave, the statements I gave, are mine and authentic. A man with my world views and my experience, an educator, was certainly able to answer a certain number of questions that are relevant to Srbac and further afield, the whole context and Karadzic's role. So it was a coincidence that I anticipated the questions. I knew what I was going to say about the situation in the municipality, about the relationship in the authorities in the municipality, and dealing with everyday issues when you don't have a state you have a war going on, you have no telephone communication with the authorities further up. Municipalities --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Milincic --

utterances.speaker: MILOS MILINCIC
utterances.text: -- were states on a small scale.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: -- you've answered the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Can I turn to paragraph 22, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the transcript, page 72, line 5, I understand why the interpreter made the mistake, the words are very similar, sound very similar. The witness didn't say: "I'm a man in good health." He said: "I'm a mature person."

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: You see paragraph 22 of your statement, last paragraph: "As president of the Srbac Municipal Assembly and member of the SDS Main Board, and based on direct contacts ... I can categorically state ..." et cetera. You see that one?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MILINCIC
utterances.text: Mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Great.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Can we have 65 ter --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Look at it quickly, please, because I'm going to turn to another document.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Can we have 65 ter 25776, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Now, here we see that same paragraph, paragraph 22 of your statement, and we also see paragraph 19 of the statement of Witness Dragomir Ljubojevic, whose evidence was admitted here earlier. He wasn't president of the Srbac Municipal Assembly, he was president of the Bijeljina Municipal Assembly. And look at the portion, Mr. Milincic, which begins: "A na osnovu ..." Now, I can read it out so you can follow, but it is verbatim, one word after another, what is provided in your statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: I object, Mr. President. First of all, it's -- at least -- unless the translation is different than --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Look at the Serbian, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, I'm looking at the Serbian, yes. I don't see it being verbatim. But, Mr. President --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Then I'll read it out and the witness can follow.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Okay. Can I finish my intervention, Mr. Tieger?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. President, the only way that this cross-examination could be relevant is if the statement is admitted because this is now an issue of whether or not what he said in the statement is his own words. And you have already said that the statement was not part of the testimony, so I'm at this time moving that the statement be admitted. Then Mr. Tieger can ask all the questions he would like about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you. That's -- what is relevant -- the statement in its entirety is not relevant for its substance. What is relevant is whether or not answers were suggested to this witness. So this paragraph is certainly relevant, and the issue of whether or not any information was provided to him, funneled to him, is relevant for purposes of assessing his testimony, but that certainly doesn't bootstrap the remainder of the statement into evidence. Quite the contrary. It casts the rest of it into doubt as well. But this paragraph is relevant; the rest of the statement is not for that purpose.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BAIRD
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, can we have some elaboration on the last point you made to the Chamber, as respects why the Chamber should not receive the entirety of the statement?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, yes, Mr. President. I have isolated this particular portion to demonstrate the proposition that this witness appears to have been provided either the specific information or the way in which he should formulate -- by the way, perhaps the witness should take off his headphones for this or leave the courtroom during this discussion. Because I have more questions for him on this issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. If Mr. Milincic, if you could excuse yourself for a moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. And -- and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Oh, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: -- I was still responding to Judge Baird's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BAIRD
utterances.text: So sorry, I thought you were waiting for the translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Oh, no. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BAIRD
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And I want to point out I'm addressing this as a matter of principle. I'm not frightened of what the -- of the statement itself. But the point is, I drew the Court's attention to this paragraph because it demonstrates some kind of inescapable conclusion, and that is that either the information itself or the formulation of that information was clearly provided to this witness, unless we are to believe in the most extraordinary coincidence of all time. Now, that makes this paragraph relevant, as the -- as paragraph 19 in the Ljubojevic statement is relevant. But how that bears on the remainder of the statement, which may or may not have reflected portions of the witness's independent knowledge, is well beyond me. The fact is that this paragraph, if anything, casts further doubt on the reliability of that statement, a statement which the Court has already ruled is in most respects irrelevant to the case itself. So it's difficult for me to see how you take a statement which the Court has already determined to be largely irrelevant and then somehow resurrect it into something relevant by virtue of the fact that one portion of it is shown to be highly suspect. If anything, it is a greater reason for not --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: When -- I don't take -- I don't think when Mr. Robinson suggested admission of the document -- statement in its entirety, it is not for the content of the statement, whether -- to make an observation whether the answers were fair to the witness, the way in which the statements were formulated.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: But, Your Honour -- Mr. President, I'm not concerned with the way paragraph 1, 2, or 3 was formulated. I haven't addressed that issue, and I haven't addressed it in part because --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: You said why you isolated this paragraph, but the way in which formulated has bearing on the other -- his testimony as a whole.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: If any single -- no, I don't agree with that. If any single part of his statement has been tainted, then it calls into question the entirety of what he's saying now and that is a matter of weight. But it can't be -- the taint can't be resurrected by the fact that other portions were not provided to the witness. Certainly it can damage the Court's view of it, as I believe it would in this case; but the fact that it doesn't infect the entirety item by item of a statement that has not been admitted is irrelevant. If you now know that this witness was provided information in any respect, as I believe you do from this --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: -- juxtaposition --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I'm sorry to interrupt you. Let me understand you correctly. Say this portion is -- this isolated portion is what? Let me say it's fed by the Defence team to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And then what's the effect of that?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Then the Court, when the Court -- well, I leave it to the Court to decide the effect. I know what the effect is for me --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] -- that we should consider this part is not in evidence. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Right. But it shows the nature of the process by which -- that brought this witness to the Court and the provision of information to the witness in some form, and therefore should certainly bear on the Court's assessment of his credibility as he testifies, particularly in light of other information brought to light during the course of cross-examination. So you certainly can't ignore it, I wouldn't think. I certainly wouldn't presume to tell the Court what effect it would -- it will choose ultimately to give its now awareness of what happened with respect to this witness. But it's certainly a factor that, in my submission, should not be ignored and that I think the -- indeed, the Prosecution had a responsibility to bring to your attention.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BAIRD
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, if the paragraph, as you say, casts doubt on the reliability of the statement, shouldn't that be a fortiori the case why the statement shouldn't be received?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Of course, if there had been some question about receipt of the statement, then I might -- for example, if the Court hadn't intervened earlier and said: Look, most of this statement is irrelevant, let's lead this witness's evidence live, if it had been a 92 ter submission, then I might well be arguing that the nature of this paragraph infuses the reliability of the statement to such an extent that it can't be received 92 ter. In this case, I'm only bringing it to the Court's attention in the context of the witness's viva voce testimony so that the Court has a better -- is in a better position to assess the reliability of what he testifies to viva voce by virtue of his previous interactions with the Karadzic Defence team.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BAIRD
utterances.text: Mr. Robinson, would you like a rejoinder in this?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, thank you very much, Judge Baird. Well, the Prosecution has created a straw man here by introducing this statement which is not previously admitted and then attempting to tear it down in part by showing that one paragraph may have been similar to what another witness has said. But in order for you to evaluate that now and having placed the reliability of this process including the taking of the statement in question, then the whole statement is relevant and becomes admissible. And that's my point.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour, I'll say it again. I'm not saying that the entirety of the statement was fed to this witness, the entirety of this largely irrelevant statement. What I'm saying is, we can see from paragraph 22 of his statement and paragraph 19 of a previous statement, the unmistakable conclusion that he was fed this language. Now, that bears on his credibility, particularly when he said that this -- that he provided his own words. So he's testifying to this Court now that these are all his own words. Now you know that he characterises something like this as his own words. You have useful information with which to assess his credibility, but it has nothing to do with the rest of the statement. If Mr. Robinson wants to argue that: We didn't provide him -- we didn't tell him, for example, in paragraph 1 of his statement what his name was and what his educational background was, I fully accept that. That's not the point. The point is that paragraph 22 was provided to this witness in some form and that directly impeaches the witness when he told this Court that this reflected his own words, and it also in a broader way affects or is useful to the Court in assessing his overall credibility and reliability when he testifies viva voce.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just one question for you, Mr. Robinson. Separate from the issue of credibility or reliability of this witness, does this issue not have a bearing upon the issue -- or bearing upon the overall reliability of the statement, 92 ter statement, from the Defence?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Absolutely, yes. As I understand it, Mr. Tieger is calling into question the -- whether the witness's words in this statement is his own. So the reliability of the statement is definitely in question.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: May I just -- just draw your attention to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Witness also mentioned that there could have been coincidences between what -- before he was shown these two paragraphs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We heard that. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll allow you to continue, Mr. Tieger. And as for the admission of the statement in its entirety, we'll deal with it after -- during the course of re-examination when Mr. Karadzic really tenders it. Shall we bring in the witness back.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, please continue, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Milincic, you still have this exhibit in front of you. You are not seriously claiming, are you, that this peon of praise to Dr. Karadzic by both you and Mr. Ljubojevic were arrived at independently by each of you, are you?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MILINCIC
utterances.text: Recently I have read a statement by a writer who said, a modern-day author, who wrote about somebody who was alive ten centuries ago. And he said: I caught him copying from me. The essence of my statement and the person who drafted it is identical. I believe that many witnesses with whom people talk, if you were to offer them that definition, they would say: This is him with more or less nuances. I have just looked at my statement now. My statement has been translated into the Cyrillic letter. It's just a style that is different; the essence is the same. The author looked at the contents of my statement and Ljubojevic's statement, provided this definition. But the essence is that one and the other must be the same. You think that we sing as a choir; however, the popular and common belief is that this is what Radovan Karadzic was. This is the essence. He was a law-obedient citizen. He was often criticised for being too democratic, that he talks too much instead of acting quickly. It would have been good if on all sides there were people who were able to count to 10 and then react. I'm more and more convinced that this definition is actually the essence of the person who was the former president of the republic. This is why I'm here. I'm not here to cheer and root for Radovan Karadzic. Now, if we looked at the words and if we discussed the theory of literature, we shouldn't do that. In legal terms, the author of this text, when he was listening to me and Ljubojevic, he provided his own wording. I just looked at my statement now and I can tell you that the essence is that he was a law-abiding person, that he tried to listen to everybody, that he suffered criticism from Serbian politicians for being too hesitant, for procrastinating, for not being too radical and resolute. And maybe it was for the better. I believe that one of his counterparts was similar to him, things would have gone the right way and the better way.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excellencies, can Mr. Tieger be asked to display the entire paragraph 22 and then you will see that it is not a verbatim copy.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: This is the portion that is -- but, by the way, excuse me, let me ask you a question. Were you looking at your statement outside to confirm -- to check what you had said?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MILINCIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. I wanted to see whether somebody was disloyal to my words. The essence of my statement for what I'm here for is that Radovan Karadzic was a humanist and a legalist. Very often people would say to him: Leave alone democracy, the parliamentary democracy, people are dying here. And he would respond: Let's do it slowly, and then he would quote from Njegos, who was a very clever man, who said: All of you people, you should be smart. So this is the essence of my state -- in style there are some nuances, but the essence of the statement is exactly what I said.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I tender this exhibit, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm still asking for the entire paragraph 22 to be displayed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We saw that entire paragraph 22 a minute ago. But he just -- this is an excerpt from the paragraph 22, I take it?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger showed paragraph 22 to the witness and then tender -- showed this comparative chart, this document, to the witness. If necessary, you can show that entire paragraph 22 -- or paragraph 22 in its entirety to the witness later on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we'll admit this.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It receives Exhibit Number P6565, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Milincic, earlier today you were asked about other municipalities and other presidents of municipalities who allegedly preserved peace. During the course of your testimony in the Krajisnik case, you were also asked about and testified about what happened in other municipalities in the Krajina as well. And that -- portions of that testimony are reflected, for example, at page 18439 of your Krajisnik testimony. And that actually began on a previous page where you were asked questions about what you were hearing was happening to Muslims and Croats in the Krajina municipalities in the spring and summer of 1992. At page 18439 the Presiding Judge intervened and said: "Mr. Milincic, no one asked you to tell us on matters you were responsible for. The question simply was: What did you learn at that time from others as to what happened in the Krajina to Croats and Muslims?" And you went on to say: "You have to know that those things were not in the open, they were not public, that if some things had been happening as you imply they were, this was not announced, this was not made public, it was not made known in Srbac. I could listen to the media, which was already biased, and I could listen to the stories, but I was not in the centre of all these developments. Some information reached me with a delay of six months about some crime, killing, violence, people being fired from work, but it happened on all the three sides. It depended on the municipality. It is only normal that I knew more about the Serbs and what was happening to them, but I also could not avoid hearing what was happening to the Muslims and Croats." And you go on to say especially because you later established contact with Bishop Komarica. Now, first of all, do you confirm, Mr. Milincic, that this is what you said at least initially in response to the question about what you knew at the time about what was happening to Muslims and Croats in the Krajina?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MILINCIC
utterances.text: I've already said that there were rumours about thousands upon thousands who were raped. I even quoted Bismarck who said that people lied the most during a war, during a hunt, and during elections. And all of those things were happening at the time. I was most concerned with my municipality. As for rumours which I heard, I can't tell you even now how credible those rumours were, whether things were covered up or not known. I don't know. But I'm sure that there were exaggerations or there were understatements. It was only normal in the state of war. I don't know why do you find this portion of my testimony problematic. I have to remind you of the great author Tolstoy who said that --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: No, Mr. Milincic, please, you don't have to --

utterances.speaker: MILOS MILINCIC
utterances.text: -- all the happy families are pretty much like --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Milincic, yeah, I know, you said that in your Krajisnik testimony as well. Let's focus on this for a moment. Okay? So first you said you heard some things but you didn't -- okay. I'm going to tender that portion and move on to what we later discussed in your Krajisnik testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll add this to Exhibit P6564.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Then Judge Orie continued his intervention: "Mr. Milincic" -- this is at page 18441. "Mr. Milincic, again, the only thing I'm asking you whether you heard that Muslims and Croats were killed. I'm not asking you whether you knew whether they told you where and when and how many; might the following questions," is what the transcript says. "Did you hear about Muslims and Croats --" And you say at the bottom of the page: "I heard. I heard. I heard. I heard. But I'm trying to be specific and tell you about a place. But I can't. I heard stories. I heard rumours." Can you confirm that is the exchange you had with the Presiding Judge in your testimony in the Krajisnik case?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MILINCIC
utterances.text: I would like to add to that that I heard that many Serbs had been killed both in Krajina and outside of Krajina. What's in dispute?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Milincic, we'll move a lot faster if you don't ask any questions --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Because this was not discussed in your -- in chief. Mr. Tieger was just asking you whether you confirm or you stand by what you said in Krajisnik testimony?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I heard stories. I heard rumours. This is how I defined those. I said it then and I'm repeating the same thing. But this is too isolated. When you asked me about --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- Croats and Muslims and when you omit the Serbs, this is isolated --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Transcript --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Milincic, the question was, I quote: Can you confirm that is the exchange you had with the Judge in your testimony in the Krajisnik case? You could have answered just "yes." Do you agree?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I've said it. I have put things in that context. I heard. I didn't see. I'm not claiming anything.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Please don't overlap. If you say just once, we are aware of this. Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On page 86, line 11 and line 12, the witness did not say what it says here: I said that many Serbs were killed as well. This now looks like a tu quoque and it was never meant to be that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe that this is what I said. I don't know. I believe that I said it because it was only logical for me to say that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: That's another singularly unhelpful intervention when the witness confirms that's what he said and Dr. Karadzic tries to re-interpret it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Let's move on. Mr. Milincic, when the ARK -- when the Crisis Staff of the Autonomous Region of the Krajina was formed, the presidents of municipalities were also members and you attended some of those meetings; correct? That's what you testified to in Krajisnik?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I'm asking a question.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: And, Mr. Tieger, we have a procedure in this courtroom that when there's an error in the transcript that Dr. Karadzic is allowed to bring that to everyone's attention. So you have to be patient in order to make -- allow him to make those interventions. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BAIRD
utterances.text: May I just add something to that, gentlemen of the bar, I think we should try to avoid having cross-talk at the bar table. It might not do well for overall appearances. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Judge Baird, understood, and we'll act in that fashion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Tieger. Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise, I was waiting for the interpretation to be over. On page 87, in my intervention, the mistake was repeated. I'm kindly asking you to listen to the entire today's hearing and correct it. I -- the witness said: I also heard that Serbs got killed. He didn't say what is written here. He talks about rumours. There were rumours about some people and there were rumours about others as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The reason I just let that -- let it go is because I didn't see much difference. If you have problem with the transcript, I would like you to raise it in writing later on with respect to this matter. Shall we continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Milincic -- well, let's just move to the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: If we can turn to page 18443 at the bottom, it will move quickly into 18444. "Q. And when the Crisis Staff of the Autonomous Region of Krajina was formed, the presidents of municipalities were also members and you attended some of those meetings? "A. Yes. Yes."

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: You did confirm that in the Krajisnik case; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MILINCIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And in fact, you also testified - and that's at page 18362 - that the ARK ordered Srbac to set up a Crisis Staff and you did so. You said: "At some point in 1992, we received an order from AR Krajina, and AR Krajina, once again, was an institution referring to the Krajina municipalities gravitating around Banja Luka. Banja Luka was the centre. And they suggested to us, ordered us, basically, to set up a Crisis Staff, which would see to it that life in the municipality could function as normally as possible ..." That's what you testified to in the Krajisnik case; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MILINCIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: So in light of your contact with the ARK authorities, the ARK Crisis Staff, the other presidents in the municipalities who attended such meetings, you were asked during the Krajisnik case about your opportunities to learn from those persons, from the leadership of the region and the leaders of other municipalities, what was happening. That's at 18444. And in particular, your attention was drawn to the comments of Mr. Kupresanin, a man who was also from Srbac, at the 24th Session of the Bosnian Serb Assembly. And those comments can be seen at 18445. That's when Mr. Kupresanin was saying that: "'We say that the war was not necessary in Bosnia and Herzegovina. The war in Bosnia and Herzegovina was necessary. Right now, if we were to count the population right now, there would be,' either" -- and the comment here is "either 'over' or 'about,' depending on whether it's 'preko' or 'eko' [phoen], 'there would be over a million Muslims in Bosnia and Herzegovina, Bosnia and Herzegovina would be a predominantly Serbian republic. Is war necessary in Serbia? It's a horrible thing to say that the war would be necessary in Serbia. If Serbia does not go into the war now, then in three to five years, the Albanians and Muslims will entirely legally overtake the power in Belgrade, along with the Serb opposition. This war was necessary for the Serb people." We're now on to 18447. And then you were asked: "Mr. Milincic, isn't Mr. Kupresanin in that body, before all those delegates, acknowledging the reduction of the Muslim population in Bosnia and Herzegovina, a reduction that took place through massive forcible expulsions? Isn't that what that's a reference to?" And your answer was: "Yes. Those are facts." That's a correct summary -- that's a correct account of your testimony in the Krajisnik case; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MILINCIC
utterances.text: No, no, I really can't recognise this. First I can't recognise Vojo Kupresanin's words. Why didn't you ask him? He was here. Really. And for me to confirm his statement, I really can't say that I could say anything about any facts. What are the facts? Please tell me, what are the facts here? I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Milincic, probably you missed some part of the question. This is what you testified in Krajisnik case. What Mr. Tieger read out to you is your testimony in the Krajisnik case, and you were read out the -- Mr. Kupresanin's speech and you were asked questions, whether that's what he said.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I -- I -- I really can't confirm that these are my words --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- and that I ever confirmed that. I don't know what Vojo said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. If you don't remember, that's fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: We'll tender it, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we'll receive these pages.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But, by the way, how much longer do you need to conclude your cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I'm jettisoning a great deal. I just want to finish this section and then ask about one more very short concrete matter. So I have one more section of this portion that concludes what we're doing right now to present to the witness and then ask him about one very discrete -- not even an issue, one previous statement he made.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: The questioning went on, Mr. Milincic, and then you were asked about what Mr. Karadzic had said in July of 1992, that is, what both Mr. Nedic and Mr. Karadzic said in July of 1992 at the 17th Assembly Session. I'm now on page 18448. Mr. Nedic was quoted as saying: "'... we must admit that the Muslims have been planted to us as a people whose executioners we are to be. I do not want the Serb people to be executioners, but I am also against us giving up our state, our land, and our territory.'" And then Dr. Karadzic was quoting discussing the -- his view of the Oriental mentality stemming from Islam, the concern that Serbs could not control the Muslim birth rate. And then he went on to say: "'There is truth in what Mr. Kupresanin has said,' although, as I indicated, that was a reference to Mr. Nedic, 'although nobody in Europe will say it openly' ... 'that this conflict was roused in order to eliminate the Muslims." Moving on to 18449, I asked you in the Krajisnik case wasn't this another acknowledgement of what was happening to Muslims in Bosnia and Herzegovina in May, June, and July of 1992. And your answer was: "As I am reading this, and as I'm listening to you, memories come back. But in Srbac, we ignored this. We simply deleted this. This may be the fact, but now, if you're asking me to remember what was said 12 years ago, it is impossible. And I adhere to what I said before, that all the things that followed the inflammatory speeches and the concrete things that were happening in the life, I was standing firmly on the ground with my two feet and I made sure that life was normal in Srbac." And then I asked you, Mr. Milincic: "... rather than standing firmly with your feet on the ground ... you were standing in Srbac, at best, with your eyes closed and your ears closed and ignoring everything that was happening to the Muslims and the Croats in the Krajina?" And your answer was: "What else could we do? In Srbac, I mean." And that was your testimony in 2005 to the Krajisnik Trial Chamber, wasn't it, Mr. Milincic?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MILINCIC
utterances.text: This really looks ridiculous, it sounds ridiculous. And now you're asking me or telling me that I should have intervened or that I should have been I don't know what. Who was it who was talking? Nedic? How should I know what Nedic was saying? I dealt with my misfortune in the way that I wanted to illustrate. Everybody was unhappy in their own way. In Republika Srpska we wanted to save ourselves the best we could. I don't know what Nedic said.
